children: MARKET WRAPS
STOCKS: U.S. stocks fell as the 10-year Treasury yield jumped back over 5% to the highest level since 2007.
TREASURYS: Investors sold off U.S. government debt, sending Treasury yields to new highs amid mounting concerns about inflation, rising interest rates and the Middle East conflict.
FOREX: The U.S. dollar rose against a basket of currencies Wednesday as markets bet on the Federal Reserve raising interest rates further.

COMMODITIES: Oil prices staged a rebound, pulling up from a five-session losing streak as investors weighed the prospect of improved Saudi export flows and U.S.-Iran diplomacy against the potential for further disruptions.
HEADLINES
Iran's President Says Open to Talks but Won't Bow to U.S.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Wednesday that Iran is ready
for negotiations to end the conflict with the U.S. but warned that Tehran
will never surrender to what he called Washington's bullying, or give up
its nuclear program.
Pezeshkian's remarks at the United Nations General Assembly come
during a protracted stalemate between the U.S. and Iran, with Washington
seeking to choke off Iran's economy through a naval blockade and
sanctions while Tehran continues striking at commercial vessels in the
Strait of Hormuz and regional infrastructure.
A day earlier, the U.S. and Iran said they had held indirect talks on
the sidelines of the General Assembly to discuss steps to end
hostilities.
U.S. Invites Putin to G-20 Summit at Trump Resort in Florida
The Trump administration has invited Russian President Vladimir Putin
to President Trump's resort in Florida in December to attend the Group of
20 leaders meeting, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Wednesday.
"We think it's an opportunity for him to engage not just with the
president, but with other world leaders," Rubio told reporters in New
York after meeting with Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov on the
sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly.
"We hope that's an invitation he'll accept," he added.
Fed's Barr Says More Rate Hikes Likely Needed to Return Inflation to
Target
Federal Reserve Gov. Michael Barr said further rate increases are
likely needed to ensure inflation comes down to target in a timely
fashion.
Barr expressed that he supported the Fed's decision to raise interest
rates by a quarter-percentage point last week, speaking at an event in
Chicago. He noted that risks to achieving the Fed's inflation target have
risen.
"Inflation is above our 2 percent target and not clearly trending
toward target in a timely way," a published text of his remarks said. "In
my base case, further policy adjustments are likely to be needed to
ensure inflation comes down to target in a timely fashion."
Anthropic Leaders Back Startup Developing System to Detect Biological
Threats
Two Anthropic leaders are investing in a small startup backed by Peter
Thiel that is developing hardware to detect viruses in the air, as fears
grow that artificial-intelligence systems might cause novel biological
threats.
Logan Graham, head of Anthropic's frontier red team and Sholto
Douglas, a member of its technical staff, invested in a $25 million seed
round for Redwood City-Calif.-based Pilgrim that valued it at $150
million, the company said. They invested in a personal capacity along
with Coinbase co-founder Fred Ehrsam, among other technology leaders, in
a round led by venture capital firm Buckley Ventures. Earlier investors
include Figma CEO Dylan Field.
The startup, Pilgrim, has built a 50-pound tripod-mounted hardware
device called Argus that is packed with sensors that combines air
sampling and genomic sequencing to detect biological threats, like Ebola
or anthrax. It signed an agreement with the Centers for Disease Control
and Prevention to develop an automated airborne biosurveillance system
for the U.S. and has begun deploying Argus in some parts of the country.
Disney Boosts Prices on Several Streaming Subscriptions
Disney is increasing prices on several of its streaming subscriptions,
a person familiar with the matter said, following similar moves from
rivals in recent months.
Standalone plans for the entertainment company's Disney+ and Hulu
streaming services will now cost an additional $2.50, at $21.49 a month,
the person said.
The increase puts the price of Disney's premium streaming plans more
on par with competitor Netflix, which sells its ad-free premium service
for $26.99 a month.
McDonald's Pledges $8.5 Billion in Investments to Help Franchisees
CHICAGO-McDonald's plans to invest billions of dollars to help its
franchisees make investments in equipment and their operations to better
compete with fast-food rivals.
The restaurant giant said Wednesday that it would spend around $8.5
billion to provide franchisees with rent assistance and help with capital
improvements through 2036 as part of a new corporate strategy. The
financial commitment, the company said, is in addition to its typical
capital-spending plans.
The pillars of the company's strategy, known as Next, are food taste
and quality, the consumer experience, restaurant operations and
hospitality. Executives introduced Next earlier this year and are sharing
details on its plans at an investor event Wednesday.
YouTube Is Battling Netflix Over Top Talent
Popular digital creators helped YouTube become the world's dominant
source of video. Now it is fighting to keep their loyalty.
The streaming platform, which is owned by Alphabet's Google, faces
growing competition from Netflix on turf it has controlled for two
decades. The platform known for "Stranger Things" and "KPop Demon
Hunters" is writing big checks to lure the producers of shows like "Good
Mythical Morning" and "Alan's Universe" to make Netflix their second
home.
At an event Wednesday, YouTube rolled out better tools for digital
producers that could help it to keep more of their content exclusively.
Flock Outlines New Limits on License-Plate Searches in Letter to U.S.
Senate
Flock Safety told the U.S. Senate that it has tightened the
requirements for police officers and other users to access and search its
database of billions of license plates amid growing concerns about misuse
of its divisive product.
The Atlanta-based company has made changes to the information users
provide when explaining their searches, Flock's chief legal officer said
in a letter to Sen. Josh Hawley, a Republican from Missouri. Flock has
said its cameras scan about 20 billion plates a month. While users have
always been required to justify their searches of the company's database,
the information was entered "in a free-text field," yielding answers that
weren't always specific, the company said in the letter viewed by The
Wall Street Journal.
Flock has now added a drop-down menu with standardized categories
modeled after the Federal Bureau of Investigation's data-reporting
system. Law-enforcement searches will require a case number in order to
conduct a search by the end of the year, although the system can be
bypassed in an emergency, Flock said.

TALKING POINT Meta's Muse AI Agent Triggers Worries About Brokerage Stocks Concerns about the impact of artificial intelligence on brokerage firms have repeatedly driven selloffs in those firms' stocks. On Tuesday, the sector took a licking, this time because of worries about Facebook parent Meta's new personal AI assistant, Muse.

Shares of Charles Schwab dropped 6% on Tuesday, its largest percentage decrease since April 16. LPL Financial and Raymond James Financial fell 7.4% and 3.5%, respectively, amid a broader selloff in financial stocks.

Those three stocks saw more muted activity on Wednesday, with Schwab down 0.2% early in the afternoon, LPL up 0.1%, and Raymond James down 0.3%. The Vanguard Financials ETF was down 0.1%. The benchmark S&P 500 index was down 0.8%.

Meta says Muse, which has surged to the top spot in Apple's app store, can help users with a range of tasks, including sending emails, booking travel, and making purchases. Meta unveiled Muse earlier this month.

Investors' concern about Muse centers on whether it or other AI tools may eventually help investors automatically move idle cash out of low-paying sweep accounts at brokerage firms to higher-paying options, such as high-yield savings accounts and money-market funds. That could put a dent in profits at Schwab, LPL, and other companies that generate handsome net interest income from sweep accounts. NII is the difference between what financial services companies pay in interest on customer deposits and what they earn on interest-bearing assets, such as loans.

The potential stakes for brokerage firms are higher in this elevated interest-rate environment, Truist analyst David Smith writes in a Sept. 22 research note. That means customers have stronger incentives to move idle dollars from low-paying sweep accounts to higher-yielding accounts.

There are hurdles, however, to a hypothetical "max cash sorting" scenario becoming reality, Smith says. Cash balances in sweep accounts are unlikely to go to zero because customers will want to keep dry powder handy for investing opportunities. In addition, some Schwab rivals have offered high-yield savings and brokerage accounts for years, and that hasn't meaningfully hindered Schwab's asset growth, he adds. Plus, brokerage firms aren't without options. If their profits on sweep cash drop, they can make up for it by charging more for other services.
By Andrew Welsch
